Forced Cyclic Quad

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: move four points on a circle and watch a second circle appear through four new corners.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or D, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Set the add-on angle, then tick the boxes to show the angles and the circle.
Look for the math

Four corners sit on one circle. Turn a line at A and a line at D by the same small angle until they hit the base line at E and F. A new circle then goes through A, E, F and D, however the four corners move.

Four corners on one circle

A, B, C and D start on one cyclic quadrilateral and can only slide around that circle. Angles BAC and BDC therefore stand on the same chord BC and are equal. The logic test confirms this on more than thirty thousand positions: the two angles agree every time.

The equal add-on angles

At A the ray AB is turned by the add-on angle in one direction, at D the ray DC is turned by the same angle in the other direction. Those rays meet the base line at E and F, so BAE = CDF. The circle through A, D and E also passes through F: the measured gap between F and that circle stays below a ten-millionth of the board's scale in every tested case. Because A, E, F and D share a circumcircle, the inscribed angles EAF and EDF stand on the same chord EF and are equal.

Why CAF equals BDE

Subtract the equal add-on angles from those equal angles and the page's conclusion follows: CAF = BDE. The article records the chain ADF + AEF = (ADC + CDF) + (ABF − BAE) = (ADC + ABC) + (CDF − BAE) = ADC + ABC = 180°. That sum holds when the four base points come in the order E, B, C, F, which is the picture you see at the start and whenever the add-on angle is positive. The conclusion itself holds more widely, including when both E and F lie between B and C. It can fail when E and F both fall beyond B or both beyond C on the same side: then B and C are not on the side EF of the quadrilateral, so the page's second formulation does not apply. The test counts those cases separately rather than hiding them.

When B and C meet

The page also says the conclusion survives when B and C coalesce and the line BC becomes the tangent to the circle. Testing that limit with E and F on the tangent line confirms it in more than a thousand positions. The old applet skips its drawing when B and C are closer than one pixel, so this port keeps that skip rather than pretending to draw the exact tangent.

Tick both angle boxes and set the add-on angle to zero: the diagram becomes plain overlapping lines, and dragging A still leaves angle CAF equal to angle BDE.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
